title: Janaka and the two roads
hookLine: a seeker of freedom is sent to learn it from a king in a palace
tomorrow: if the old rites were too long, what were people meant to do?

lines: SENT TO A KING, NOT A HERMIT.
cards: In the Mahabharata, young Shuka, son of the sage Vyasa, wants moksha, freedom, more than anything. So his father sends him to learn it, not from a hermit in a cave, but from a king: Janaka of Mithila.

Shuka is kept waiting at the palace gate, then lodged among gardens, music and comfort, and none of it moves him. Janaka himself is remembered for a well-known line: if Mithila burns, nothing of mine burns.
A king, in a palace, and free. So, one question today: do you have to give up enjoying life to be free?

teach.b: The Kularnava Tantra answers plainly. Usually, it says, a yogi is no enjoyer, and an enjoyer knows nothing of yoga. But the Kula way is made of both, bhoga and yoga together.
Bhoga is enjoyment, the taste of life. Yoga here is the discipline that leads to freedom.
It isn't a license; two days ago the same book was warning hard against appetite.

teach.h: JANAKA: A DOOR, NOT A DETOUR.
teach.b: It's a claim about the world: if everything is the goddess's power, tasting it with full awareness, the way Janaka lived in his palace, can be a door, not a detour. A neighbor says something close, in its own words.

In Ecclesiastes, in the Hebrew Bible that Jews and Christians both read, the King James Version has: "There is nothing better for a man, than that he should eat and drink, and that he should make his soul enjoy good in his labour. This also I saw, that it was from the hand of God."
What they share: enjoyment isn't the enemy of a holy life.
The honest difference: Ecclesiastes receives the good things as a gift from God's hand.
The Kula verse treats the enjoying itself, done with awareness, as part of the road to freedom.

how: Teachers in Kula and related tantric lineages speak of bhoga and moksha, enjoyment and liberation, as goals the practice holds together rather than apart.

games.q: what does “what tantra actually is” mean?
o: enjoying life now, and seeking freedom later
giving up every pleasure in order to be free

games.q: one question, two answers. tap the pairs.
p: a king in a palace, and free
a yogi who also enjoys: both at once
eat, drink, enjoy: from God's hand

s: in the Kula verse, you must choose enjoyment or freedom
the Kula way is made of both, bhoga and yoga together.
Vyasa sent his son Shuka to learn freedom from a king
Janaka of Mithila, who lived among comforts and was still free.
Ecclesiastes calls eating, drinking and enjoying good 'from the hand of God'
Ecclesiastes 2:24, in the King James Version.

games.q: your uncle says a serious spiritual life means skipping every celebration. what would the Kula verse say back?
o: enjoyment and discipline can be held together at once.
he's right: yoga and bhoga can never share one life.
celebrate freely; in the Kula way, discipline is optional.
games.why: in the Kula way, both are held at once, as Janaka kept a palace and his freedom. it isn't a license: the Kularnava guards hard against mere appetite.

practice: Bring to mind three good things you tasted, heard or enjoyed this week, a few breaths each. If you pray, offer each one back in your heart, the way many Hindus offer food to God before eating it.
Hold each fully for a moment, without guilt, and without reaching for more. Then let the last one go, and simply breathe.

wordCard.voice: What tantra actually is: here, a way that holds bhoga and yoga, enjoyment and discipline, together.

orig.note: Sanskrit: enjoyment, experience; paired with yoga in the Kula verse.

carryVoice: For the road: bhoga and yoga, held together. Janaka kept his palace and his freedom. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Mokshadharma (Vyasa sends Shuka to King Janaka of Mithila, who keeps him waiting and lodges him amid comforts before teaching him; Janaka's saying that if Mithila burns, nothing of his burns, also cited in the Shanti Parva)
Kularnava Tantra, chapter 2 (a yogi is not usually an enjoyer, nor an enjoyer a knower of yoga; the Kaula way is made of both bhoga and yoga)

sources.q: There is nothing better for a man, than that he should eat and drink, and that he should make his soul enjoy good in his labour. This also I saw, that it was from the hand of God.
